p68: 68.  As to the “necessity in a democratic society” of the interference, the Chamber, while stating that it was not its task to substitute itself for the domestic courts in assessing whether there was a grave risk within the meaning of Article 13 (b), considered that it had to ascertain whether, in applying and interpreting the Hague Convention, the courts had complied with the requirements of Article 8, particularly in the light of the principles established by the Court in its Neulinger and Shuruk judgment (cited above). Turning first to the psychological report drawn up at the mother’s request after the first-instance judgment, it found that the Regional Court had refused to take it into consideration on the grounds that it concerned the issue of custody of the child and that the child would be protected by Australian legislation. In its view, while the fact that the child had not been heard did not pose a problem given her age, the Regional Court should nevertheless have examined the conclusions of the psychological certificate, together with the objections raised by the “Bāriņtiesa”, in addition to which nothing had prevented it from ordering a psychological expert report of its own motion.
p69: 69.  The Chamber then indicated that the courts should also have satisfied themselves that there were other sufficient safeguards for the return to take place in the best possible conditions for the child, in particular as regards her material living conditions in Australia, and as regards the possibility for the applicant to follow her daughter and to maintain contact with her.
p70: 70.  While observing that the Latvian courts’ decision in this case contrasted with other proceedings conducted in Latvia (see Šneersone and Kampanella v. Italy, no. 14737/09, § 94, 12 July 2011), and after rejecting the Government’s argument that the applicant had failed to cooperate and noting the traumatic manner in which the decision had been enforced, the Chamber concluded that an in-depth examination of the entire family situation and of a whole series of factors had been lacking in the approach taken by the Latvian courts and that, accordingly, the interference had been disproportionate within the meaning of Article 8.
p71: 71.  The applicant considered that the Chamber judgment was exemplary in assisting the domestic authorities in their search for the best interests of the child. She noted that, while the Government complained in their request for referral to the Grand Chamber that the Chamber had not had at its disposal all the documents examined by the domestic courts, it had been for them to produce those documents. In her view, the domestic authorities had not sought to give precedence to the best interests of the child. She considered that only psychological expert reports could determine the best interests of the child: in the present case, however, the domestic courts had refused to examine the psychological report she had produced, thereby breaching Article 12 of the International Convention on the Rights of the Child (hearing of the child, either directly or through a representative or an appropriate body). She emphasised that in determining those “best interests”, several factors related to the child’s situation and to the situation and abilities of the persons potentially responsible for the child were generally taken into account, the protection and well-being of the child being paramount.
p72: 72.  The applicant added that in applying to the Court her main aim had been to challenge the position taken by the domestic courts in various cases concerning the Hague Convention and to show the need to secure the best interests of the child.
p73: 73.  The Government noted that the Court imposed a number of obligations on the domestic authorities, in particular: to ensure that parents were involved in the proceedings to a degree sufficient to protect their interests (see Iosub Caras v. Romania, no. 7198/04, § 41, 27 July 2006); to prevent further harm to the child or prejudice to the interested parties as provided for in Article 7 of the Hague Convention (ibid., § 34, and Ignaccolo-Zenide v. Romania, no. 31679/96, § 99, ECHR 2000-I); to deal urgently with proceedings concerning the return of an abducted child, including the enforcement of the decisions given (see Carlson v. Switzerland, no. 49492/06, § 69, 6 November 2008); and to provide redress to the applicant parent in the event of failure to comply with the six-week time-limit laid down in Article 11 of the Hague Convention (ibid., § 55).
